title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context. The previous page solved a plane problem: find algebraic curves whose arc length s is not algebraic but depends on a prescribed quadrature ∫P dp, possibly vanishing for chosen arcs. Euler did this by writing the curve as the envelope of lines y = nx + p with s = x√(1+nn) + q, so that dp/dq becomes the key relation. He now treats the 'problema principale' on the unit sphere: dx² sin²y + dy² = dr², with x = longitude, y = colatitude and r = arc length. All three are circular arcs whose sines and cosines are to be algebraic. He proceeds 'retrogradely'.

Step 1 (the dy-part). Write dx sin y = dr sin ω and dy = dr cos ω, so ω is the course angle. Then make the ansatz cos ω sin y = p cos r + q sin r, with p and q independent of r explicitly. One wants sin y dy = (p cos r + q sin r) dr to integrate as cos y = q cos r − p sin r. Differentiating, this holds exactly when sin r dp − cos r dq = 0, i.e. tan r = dq/dp. This is the spherical analogue of the envelope/Legendre trick of the plane case: a one-parameter family in (p, q) whose envelope condition fixes r.

Step 2. From this, sin²y = 1 + 2pq sin r cos r − qq cos²r − pp sin²r and cos ω = (p cos r + q sin r)/sin y. Then sin²ω sin²y = sin²y − (p cos r + q sin r)² = 1 − pp − qq. Hence sin ω = √(1−pp−qq)/sin y and dx = dr/√(1−pp−qq). Note that (p, q, √(1−pp−qq)) is a unit vector: in effect the pole expressed in a frame rotating with the curve.

Step 3 (parenthesis). Comparison with an earlier solution in angles θ, ψ gives q = cos θ and p = −sin θ cos ψ. This reproduces cos ω = (cos θ sin r − sin θ cos r cos ψ)/sin y and tan r = dθ sin θ / d(sin θ cos ψ). In that solution dx = dξ + dφ with dφ = dθ/(tan ψ sin θ) = p dq/((1−qq)√(1−pp−qq)). With q as independent variable, dr = −dq ddp/(dp²+dq²). Euler then forms dξ and asserts it is the differential of an arc with cot ξ = ((dp/dq)(1−qq) + pq)/√(1−pp−qq). He breaks off: 'evolutio nimis difficilis'.

Step 4 ('Aliud tentamen'). Set dx = dξ + dφ and divide by sin²ξ, requiring d(−cot ξ) to be integrable. On the next page he puts −cot ξ = −u cot r + t with u, t free of r. Evaluating at r = 0 and r = 90° gives u = (1−qq)/√(1−pp−qq) and t = −pq/√(1−pp−qq). One can check that with these values the required relation W(uu cos²r − 2tu sin r cos r + (1+tt) sin²r) = u sin²y holds identically in r, where W = √(1−pp−qq). So the cot ξ of the parenthesis is recovered. What remains is to make φ an arc with algebraic trigonometric functions.

Purpose. The aim is to construct algebraic spherical curves whose arc length is a circular arc with algebraic sine and cosine (or a prescribed transcendental), parallel to the plane construction.
errors: Sign slip in dξ. Since dφ = +p dq/((1−qq)W), one has dξ = dx − dφ = (1/W)(−dq ddp/(dq²+dp²) − p dq/(1−qq)). Euler writes +p dq/(1−qq), and the combined numerator inherits this sign; with the minus sign on that term the combined numerator would read −(p dq³ + p dp² dq + dq ddp − qq dq ddp).
Euler implicitly takes q as independent variable (ddq = 0) when writing dr = −dq ddp/(dq²+dp²); this is unstated.

The claim that dξ is the differential of the arc with the stated cotangent is asserted, not verified. I could not confirm it quickly (1 + cot²ξ does not reduce simply to the stated denominator). Euler himself abandons the computation.

Next page (context): the condition is written with factor (1−pp−qq) where it should be √(1−pp−qq), since sin ω sin y = W. The subsequent use is correct, and the found u, t make the condition an identity in r. Determining them only from r = 0 and r = 90° is merely a necessary condition, but it happens to suffice here.

ideas.what: Ansatz cos y = q cos r − p sin r with envelope condition tan r = dq/dp, making the latitude relation integrable algebraically
ideas.modern_name: Spherical analogue of the support-function / Legendre-envelope representation of a curve
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (plane version; envelope methods for rectifiable curves); support function later Minkowski
ideas.where_published: Euler's published papers on algebraic curves rectifiable by circular arcs and on spherical rectifiable curves (exact E-numbers unsure)

ideas.what: Identity sin²ω sin²y = 1 − p² − q², giving dx = dr/√(1−pp−qq); (p, q, √(1−pp−qq)) is a unit vector
ideas.modern_name: Pole expressed in a moving orthonormal frame along a spherical curve

ideas.what: Splitting dx = dξ + dφ and forcing d(cot ξ) to be linear in cot r, with coefficients found by evaluating at r = 0 and r = 90°

missed.claim: Euler sets up a general parametrisation, by an arbitrary pair p(q), of spherical curves whose latitude part integrates algebraically, but leaves the longitude part (φ algebraic) unresolved.
missed.quote: Quarum formularum evolutio nimis est difficilis
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is a historical precursor of constructing spherical curves with algebraic (Pythagorean-hodograph-like) arc length. This is mildly interesting for the history of rectifiable spherical curves, but the theme is known from Euler's published work.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working draft of the spherical rectification problem that Euler treated in published papers. The envelope ansatz and the unit-vector identity are neat but natural, and the page ends in an abandoned computation containing a sign slip.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image essentially; 'tang' = tan.
In the parenthesis the dξ bracket is printed with + p dq/(1−qq) (a printed or derivational sign error, not an OCR error).
